title: Destroying Enemies by Making Them Friends: Sublime Grace
summary: When a vengeful lady asked why he did not destroy the defeated rebels, Lincoln replied: 'Do I not destroy my enemies when I make them my friends?'
keywords: Destroying Enemies by Making Them Friends: Sublime Grace
full_text:
In April 1865, after four agonizing years of carnage, the American Civil War came to an end with General Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox.

In Washington, bloodthirsty politicians and vengeful citizens demanded that southern leaders be executed and Confederate states subjected to brutal military subjugation.

At a White House reception, an outraged socialite approached President Lincoln:
"Mr. President! Why do you speak of reconciliation and charity toward the south? They are traitors! Is it not your duty as Commander-in-Chief to utterly destroy your enemies?"

Lincoln looked at the woman with deep, sorrowful compassion. His voice was gentle yet piercing:

**"Madam! Do I not destroy my enemies when I make them my friends?"**

The woman stood silenced by the grandeur of the thought.

Lincoln added softly:
"We have conquered on the battlefield; now we must conquer their hearts.
Vengeance will only breed future rebellions and perpetual hatred.
Only charity toward all and malice toward none can heal this broken land."

Lincoln's sublime ethic of transforming enemies through forgiveness remains the pinnacle of democratic statesmanship.
moral: Retaliation perpetuates hatred; true victory is achieved when former adversaries are reconciled through magnanimity.
